transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-06 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Aisha Patel (Redwood SE), Marta Li (Redwood CSM), Mark Rivera (HaloHealth CTO), Sofia Chen (HaloHealth SRE Lead), David Kim (HaloHealth PM), Lena Ortiz (HaloHealth Security)

Summary: quick handoff after last week's production fallback storm. goal is align on root cause, short-term mitigations, and a remediation sprint. references: RCA draft (private link) https://redwood.internal/notes/halohealth-rca, perf traces: https://perf.redwood/halo-traces-2025-08-01

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Hayes: All right everyone, thanks for hopping on. we'll give it a minute for folks to join but, um, main purpose is to walk through the RCA quick and hand off the mitigation tasks. uh Marta you're on for customer success notes.
[00:27] Marta Li: Yep hi all, recording on and i'll capture action items.
[00:35] Mark Rivera: Thanks. quick note: we had two major fallback events last wed during the morning peak, about - we saw a 7x increase in fallback rate on the /generate route. that basically doubled our latency tail and had some user impact.
[01:14] Aisha Patel: Thanks, Mark. just to level set: from Redwood's side we saw the evictions in the prefix/KV cache paired with a sudden shift in token distribution — long contexts — and then concurrent autoscale cold starts. the runtime started evicting persisted prefixes which caused more token decode and a cascade into fallback.
[01:45] Sofia Chen: i had noticed the eviction metric go from normal to spike in maybe five minutes. the eviction ratio hit 0.42 which is way above our expected 0.05. it lined up with a batch size jump because one of our batchers had a backlog.
[02:20] David Kim: can you explain the sequence again? i heard cache eviction -> fallback but why did fallback rates keep climbing after eviction stopped?
[02:45] Aisha Patel: good question. two things: first, once prefixes are evicted the downstream requests are heavier — more kv fetches and longer decode — so the per-request GPU time increases which reduces throughput; second, our autoscaler reacted but with conservative cooldowns so restored capacity lagged. while the autoscaler warmed up, the backlog increased, which in turn caused more eviction pressure — a positive feedback loop.
[03:30] Jordan Hayes: and to add — there was a model fallback policy set to "latency-first" for that environment; once latency crossed threshold, requests were sent to a lower-capacity fallback model which can't handle the same concurrency and so latencies ratcheted up further. it's an unfortunate chain.
[04:05] Mark Rivera: okay, timeline makes sense. did we see any storage or network flakiness that triggered eviction? or was it purely memory pressure on the GPU pods?
[04:33] Aisha Patel: preliminary traces show normal network, and storage iops were fine. this was memory/kv pressure. we also observed an unusual prompt pattern from a smaller subset of users — long trial runs with many system tokens. that increased average sequence lengths by about 40%.
[05:05] Lena Ortiz: from security's perspective i want to confirm no user data leaked during fallbacks, that fallback model uses same data handling policies, and audit logs are preserved. Jordan, Marta — is that captured in the RCA?
[05:30] Jordan Hayes: yes. RCA has a section — short version: no PII was transmitted outside our control plane, fallbacks were internal model variants; audit logs kept. we'll attach the log export to the doc.
[06:02] Marta Li: adding: lena we'll loop you in on the exports.
[06:10] Sofia Chen: on metrics, the token processing time per request jumped from 120ms to 420ms median for the affected cohort. that explains the throughput drop more than the absolute failed requests.
[06:42] Aisha Patel: we ran a quick repro in staging: replaying the long-context traffic with identical batching led to the same eviction pattern. then we doubled cache capacity and the eviction rate stayed below 0.08 and throughput recovered. so capacity tuning helps.
[07:20] David Kim: are there config knobs we can set right now to avoid immediate recurrence while we plan remediation?
[07:38] Aisha Patel: yes, three short-term mitigations: 1) raise prefix/KV cache quota for the cluster, 2) relax autoscaler cooldowns for that worker pool, 3) temporarily change the routing policy to favor capacity-first model variant (instead of latency-first). together these should blunt the feedback loop.
[08:14] Mark Rivera: procurement may take a day but we can approve temporary quota bump for 72 hours. need a PR from you, Jordan.
[08:28] Jordan Hayes: will do. i'll send a request for the 72-hr burst and the cost estimate in the follow-up email.
[08:40] Marta Li: note, we'll also include the security checklist so Lena can sign off quickly.
[08:55] Lena Ortiz: appreciate that. also curious about the fallback model's tokenization differences — could a tokenizer mismatch cause the longer contexts?
[09:15] Aisha Patel: tokenizer mismatch was checked — models use same tokenizer family; the longer contexts came from user prompts: a change in the onboarding flow caused customers to include more system text in each request.
[09:40] David Kim: oh that was our experiment last month. okay, we rolled that to a subset — didn't realize it would spike token lengths at scale. my bad.
[09:55] Mark Rivera: so we have an operational mitigation and an application-level fix (roll back or change onboarding). what's the priority and who owns the rollout?
[10:12] David Kim: product will roll back the experiment to the smaller cohort and change the onboarding text by EOD tomorrow unless infra asks otherwise.
[10:30] Sofia Chen: for the remediation sprint we should include an autoscaler policy change (shorter cooldowns), a cache-size increase, and a bake test that replays the long-context traffic.
[10:52] Aisha Patel: Agreed. also suggest adding a circuit-breaker at the ingress that throttles sessions if sequence length > X to protect the runtime while we fix upstream prompts.
[11:12] Jordan Hayes: quick note on observability: we'll share a dashboard and a tracer link with the KV eviction timeline. Marta will attach to the RCA.
[11:30] Marta Li: noted.
[11:40] Mark Rivera: regarding the fallback config — can we change from automatic fallback to an incremental degrade that slows token rate rather than switching models?
[11:58] Aisha Patel: that's possible but requires a small runtime change; we have a knob called "graceful-fallthrough" that does soft degradation. enabling it should be safe in canary first. we can flip in 24-48 hours.
[12:20] Sofia Chen: can we do canary to 10% of traffic for 6 hours and monitor tail latency?
[12:35] Aisha Patel: yes that's our recommended pattern. we'll coordinate the canary with you.
[12:45] Lena Ortiz: about audit — i need to confirm retention windows for logs. what's the retention now?
[12:57] Jordan Hayes: by default 30 days for request traces, but we can extend exports for compliance. we'll include an export package for the incident window.
[13:18] David Kim: curious — do you think quantization or model size choices affected this?
[13:30] Aisha Patel: not directly for this incident. quantization can affect per-token latency slightly, but the root was cache eviction and autoscale lag. the fallback model being smaller did exacerbate tail latency.
[13:55] Mark Rivera: do we have any temporary throttling we can apply from the app side to smooth the burst while infra stabilizes?
[14:10] Sofia Chen: yes we can add a client-side rate limit on requests per session and early reject or return a friendly backoff message.
[14:22] David Kim: we'll implement a soft throttle and measure impact; product will own that change.
[14:35] Jordan Hayes: i'm going to walk through the immediate timeline: today — send RCA + cost estimate for burst; 72 hrs after approval — Redwood will enable burst quota and canary graceful-fallthrough; within 48 hrs — SE-run KV-cache replay tests and post results; next week — 2-hour remediation sprint to tune autoscaler and bake changes; timeline sounds okay?
[15:10] Mark Rivera: sounds good. can we get a more granular risk/impact breakdown in the RCA? e.g. number of affected users, user segments, and estimated revenue impact.
[15:28] Jordan Hayes: yes will add that. initial estimate is <0.5% daily active users for the window, but we'll verify.
[15:40] Marta Li: action items recap: Jordan send RCA + burst PR; Aisha run replay tests; Sofia provision staging nodes; Mark confirm procurement; David roll back onboarding or change text; Lena verify audit export.
[16:05] Mark Rivera: a few technical follow-ups — 1) can you share the exact autoscaler parameters you saw, 2) which model variant was fallbacking, 3) is there a ticket for the graceful-fallthrough runtime change?
[16:25] Aisha Patel: sure: autoscaler parameters: target_cpu 60%, cooldown 5m (we recommend 60s for that pool), min_replicas 2, max 20. fallback variant: rdl-medea-small-v2. and yes we have an internal ticket RDW-1892 for graceful-fallthrough; i'll link it.
[17:00] David Kim: rdl-medea-small-v2 — can we pin a higher-capacity variant just for this customer while the fix is in progress? even if it's costlier.
[17:15] Jordan Hayes: we can do a temporary pin to rdl-medea-medium-quant. need approval from procurement for the cost delta; i'll include numbers.
[17:28] Mark Rivera: approve for 72 hours if cost is reasonable. please include an estimate.
[17:40] Marta Li: i'll note that in the action items.
[17:50] Lena Ortiz: on security, i want the export to include request IDs and redaction for user content. no raw user messages in the export.
[18:05] Jordan Hayes: understood. we'll redact user content and include request IDs and metadata only.
[18:20] Sofia Chen: SE question: any concern with KV cache resizing causing restart of pods? we prefer not to cause restarts during high traffic.
[18:33] Aisha Patel: resizing can be done live by increasing the memory allocation on the node-pool; if that's not possible without restart we can instead do a rolling scale up to add capacity and let the runtime allocate more cache slots — no full cluster restart required.
[18:55] Mark Rivera: good. next, on longer-term mitigations — what should we prioritize?
[19:10] Aisha Patel: long-term: 1) add sequence-length-based ingress throttles; 2) bake in KV cache autoscaling heuristics; 3) tighter autoscaler configs by workload; 4) enrich canary tests with long-context replay.
[19:35] David Kim: we'll add a ticket to product backlog for onboarding change and throttle work.
[19:45] Jordan Hayes: i'll include the long-term roadmap items in the RCA and propose a joint quarter plan for them.
[20:00] Marta Li: quick note — someone asked earlier about whether this incident affects compliance posture for existing SOC2 controls. Lena?
[20:12] Lena Ortiz: at a glance it doesn't change control effectiveness; we need the audit export and confirmation that PII was never exported. after that i'm comfortable.
[20:30] Jordan Hayes: we'll get that to you.
[20:40] Aisha Patel: small gotcha in the staging replay — we saw a small discrepancy because the staging policy used a different batching window; we'll standardize the replay to match prod batching.
[21:00] Sofia Chen: timeline for that standardization?
[21:07] Aisha Patel: 24 hours. we'll post the updated test config to the incident repo.
[21:20] Mark Rivera: can SE also include the raw trace IDs so we can slice by user segment?
[21:30] Aisha Patel: yes we'll provide trace IDs and mapping to impacted segments.
[21:45] David Kim: anything else before we go into the remediation scheduling?
[21:52] Jordan Hayes: one more: we recommend a 6-hour watch window after the canary flip with Redwood engineers on call. Marta will coordinate calendars.
[22:07] Marta Li: noted. i'll add calendar invites for the 6-hour watch and the remediation sprint.
[22:20] Mark Rivera: for the remediation sprint can we get an agenda and pre-read 24 hours ahead?
[22:30] Jordan Hayes: yes. agenda: root cause walk, config changes, staging bake results, canary plan, rollback plan. pre-read includes RCA, replay results, autoscaler params.
[22:45] Lena Ortiz: and security pre-read: audit export and redaction verification.
[22:55] Jordan Hayes: we'll send all that.
[23:05] Sofia Chen: quick note on observability retention — can we extend traces for the incident window to 90 days temporarily?
[23:18] Jordan Hayes: yes we can export and store them off-platform; cost will be included in the burst PR.
[23:32] David Kim: good.
[23:40] Jordan Hayes: any pushback on the canary percent or duration?
[23:48] Sofia Chen: 10% for 6 hours with on-call watch is fine.
[24:00] Mark Rivera: agreed.
[24:12] Jordan Hayes: all right, to close — recap of deliverables and owners will be in the follow-up email. Marta will circulate the RCA link and the calendar invites. anyone want to add a last-minute item?
[24:30] David Kim: just a request that we get a cost estimate breakdown for pinning a higher-capacity model variant — include per-hour delta.
[24:40] Jordan Hayes: will include.
[24:48] Marta Li: i've captured that.
[25:00] Jordan Hayes: cool. thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the RCA and concrete PR.
[25:08] Mark Rivera: thanks all.
[25:12] Lena Ortiz: thanks.
[25:18] Sofia Chen: bye.
[25:22] Marta Li: ending recording.

Notes on transcript quality: Some speaker overlaps, and timestamps are approximate. There were a few places where product names were mistranscribed (e.g., rdl-medea vs medea-small) — RCA will include canonical names.

References attached: RCA (private): https://redwood.internal/notes/halohealth-rca, Traces: https://perf.redwood/halo-traces-2025-08-01, Internal ticket: https://redwood.internal/tickets/RDW-1892

End of transcript.
